detail.abstract: Introduction: Myanmar migrant workers in Thailand face elevated tuberculosis (TB) risk due to crowded living conditions, labor-intensive work, and limited access to healthcare. Health insurance may influence care-seeking behavior and treatment completion, yet evidence among this population is limited. The objectives of this study are: 1) to assess the extent to which health insurance status is associated with intended care-seeking behavior for tuberculosis diagnosis among migrants when developing symptoms, and; 2) to assess the extent to which health insurance status is associated with the intention to receive the full course of treatment for tuberculosis in Thailand if given the diagnosis Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional study among 330 Myanmar migrant factory workers using a self-administered questionnaire written in Myanmar language. Key outcomes included intention to seek formal healthcare if TB symptoms developed and intention to complete the full course of TB treatment if diagnosed. We used logistic regression analyses to assess the association between the exposure and outcomes with adjustment for age, sex, income, education, marital status, length of stay in Thailand, and TB history. Results: Most participants reported that they had health insurance (96.1%), and threequarters (73.3%) reported that they would seek formal healthcare if they developed TB symptoms, and more than four-fifths (83.6%) reported that they would complete the full course of TB treatment in Thailand if diagnosed. Uninsured participants were more likely to not seek formal care (37.5% vs. 17.5%; Adjusted OR = 4.71, 95% CI = 0.60, 36.88). All uninsured respondents who answered the treatment question indicated they would complete the full treatment. Conclusion: Uninsured workers were less likely to seek formal care than insured workers when they developed TB symptoms, but were universally intent on staying in Thailand for the full course of treatment if diagnosed with TB. Limitations regarding the measurement question, selection bias, and information bias should be considered in the interpretation of the study findings.

title: Fiat-Collateralized Stablecoins Driving the Development of DeFi and the Metaverse: An Analysis Based on Compliance, Technological Synergy, and Liquidity
affiliations: Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, Guangxi University of Finance and Economics, Zhaoqing University and Quzhou University

detail.title: Fiat-Collateralized Stablecoins Driving the Development of DeFi and the Metaverse: An Analysis Based on Compliance, Technological Synergy, and Liquidity
detail.abstract: Major economies throughout the world have enacted legislation for stablecoins, and their market value has skyrocketed. When it comes to the worlds of decentralized finance and the metaverse, stablecoins are being more acknowledged as having a significant influence. A qualitative investigation of the ways in which stablecoins contribute to the expansion of decentralized finance and the metaverse is carried out in this study. The investigation makes use of data from DeFiLlama as well as relevant case studies. Results show that stablecoins activate liquidity, promote technological synergy, and ease compliance, all of which contribute to the advancement of decentralized finance and the metaverse. Additional research reveals that many stakeholders in stablecoins have their own distinct approaches to capture value. This research advances the understanding of how stablecoins achieve growth, identifies key drivers behind the development of the metaverse and decentralized finance (DeFi), and proposes pathways to overcome critical barriers to industry expansion.

title: Beyond the Prototype: The Interaction of Entrepreneur Appearance and Prototype Quality in Electronics Startup Funding
affiliations: , Afe Babalola University,  and

detail.title: Beyond the Prototype: The Interaction of Entrepreneur Appearance and Prototype Quality in Electronics Startup Funding
detail.abstract: Abstract:This study explores how entrepreneur appearance and prototype quality jointly influence funding outcomes in early stage electronics and hardware startups. We investigate whether the influence of appearance is amplified or reduced when tangible, technically sophisticated prototypes are presented to investors. Drawing on data from over 600 startup pitch observations across competitions, accelerators, and online media, the study measures appearance (rated 6–10), prototype quality (partial vs. functional), and their interaction, with funding success as the outcome variable. Results reveal high appearance ratings and balanced prototype distributions. Correlation matrix shows associations without possible collinearity. Logistic and ordinal regression results show that neither appearance, prototype quality, nor their interaction significantly predict funding outcomes. Even after accounting for event type, year, sector, and founder or team-level factors, the models exhibit weak explanatory power (pseudo-R² < 0.03; ROC = 0.635). These findings suggest that in highly technical and capital-intensive contexts, investors prioritize substantive signals of feasibility and competence over visual or surface cues. The study contributes to research on entrepreneurial signalling and investor decision-making by highlighting the boundary conditions under which appearance effects are attenuated in technology-based ventures.

title: Exploring Low-Carbon Transportation Pathways in Inner Mongolia Based on GDIM-STIRPAT Models
affiliations: Inner Mongolia University and

detail.title: Exploring Low-Carbon Transportation Pathways in Inner Mongolia Based on GDIM-STIRPAT Models
detail.abstract: To support carbon peaking in Inner Mongolia's transportation sector and promote low-carbon development, this study examines the evolution, drivers, decoupling trends, and future scenarios of transportation carbon emissions. Using the GDIM model, decoupling effort model, and an extended STIRPAT model with ridge regression, the analysis reveals that economic growth is the main driver of emissions, while energy consumption and intensity are key restraining factors. The decoupling effort model highlights a policy cycle pattern between emissions and economic growth, emphasizing the need for consistent policy measures. Scenario forecasts based on the STIRPAT model predict continued emission growth until 2030, followed by a gradual decline. The greatest reductions occur under scenarios with optimized energy structures and improved energy efficiency. These findings provide a scientific basis for policy recommendations to help achieve Inner Mongolia’s dual carbon goals.

title: The effect patterns of the built environment on shared e-bike ridership: Evidence from 36 Chinese cities
affiliations: Zhejiang University and Zhejiang University

detail.title: The effect patterns of the built environment on shared e-bike ridership: Evidence from 36 Chinese cities
detail.abstract: The expansion of shared e-bike services has fostered growing interest in the relationship between shared e-bike ridership and the urban built environment. However, existing research mainly focuses on bike-sharing and relies on single-city case studies, limiting insights into the varying effects of the built environment across multiple cities. To address this limitation and provide guidance for optimising shared e-bike services, this study conducts a nationwide analysis to examine heterogeneous built-environment effect patterns on shared e-bike ridership using trip data from 36 Chinese cities. We employ interpretable ensemble regression models and Shapley Additive Explanations to quantify the relative importance of built environment variables in each city. Principal component analysis and K-Means++ clustering are then used to identify typical effect patterns, with non-parametric tests revealing significant inter-group differences. The key findings are twofold. First, leisure and retail facilities exhibit the highest relative importance in most cities, followed by residential facilities, whereas road-network characteristics are generally of lower importance. the relative-importance profiles also vary by city type. Second, five typical effect patterns are identified: retail-dominated, leisure-dominated, balanced amenity-employment, residential-dominated, and central proximity-dominated. Non-parametric tests confirm significant inter-group differences in relative importance: land-use mix is higher in retail- and central proximity-dominated patterns; leisure facilities are higher in residential-dominated than in central proximity-dominated patterns; and employment facilities are higher in central proximity-dominated than in retail-dominated patterns. These findings underscore the context-dependent nature of built environment influences, informing tailored urban planning for e-bike-sharing services and sustainable mobility.

title: The Many Faces of Proactiveness: Insights from Russian SMEs
affiliations: National Research University – Higher School of Economics (HSE University), ,  and Bentley University

detail.title: The Many Faces of Proactiveness: Insights from Russian SMEs
detail.abstract: Proactiveness is an essential construct in entrepreneurship and organizational behavior research, linked to individual and organizational effectiveness. Yet, despite its extensive study, how proactiveness is understood and manifested across cultural contexts remains underexplored. This study examines the manifestations and meaning of proactiveness in the organizational settings within Russia's unique historical, institutional, and socio-cultural context. Through qualitative analysis of 18 Russian SMEs, we identify distinct dimensions of proactiveness at three levels – the executive, the employee, and the firm level. The study reveals how contextual factors, including Soviet-era legacies and high uncertainty avoidance, shape proactive behaviors and strategic choices. By integrating imprinting theory, we also demonstrate how deeply rooted imprints persist and influence behaviors in turbulent environments. This study contributes to the entrepreneurship and management literature by nuancing the construct of proactiveness in non-Western settings and highlighting implications for managing proactive behaviors in institutionally complex contexts.

title: How measures for greenhouse gas mitigation in agriculture are implemented strongly determines cost-effectiveness
affiliations: Agroscope, Agroscope, Agroscope, Government of the Swiss Confederation - Agroscope Reckenholz-Tänikon Research Station, Agroscope and Agroscope

detail.title: How measures for greenhouse gas mitigation in agriculture are implemented strongly determines cost-effectiveness
detail.abstract: To reach the net-zero emission target, Switzerland aims to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions of the agricultural sector by 40% relative to 1990 levels. However, recent stagnation in emission reductions highlights the urgent need for further cost-effective mitigation and carbon sequestration measures. The Marginal Abatement Cost Curve (MACC) is a widely used tool to identify such measures. Nevertheless, its outcomes are highly sensitive to the underlying assumptions of measure implementation, which are rarely discussed appropriately.This study identified twelve potential measures, with up to three different scenarios each (i.e., implementation assumptions). Costs and mitigation potentials of each measure and scenario were quantified. The scenarios were classified into three categories—most realistic, low-cost, and high-cost—and three separate MACCs were constructed.Our findings reveal that variation in assumptions of measure implementation significantly affects MACC outcomes—particularly in measure prioritization, cost-effective measures, budget requirements (118–1,133 Mio CHF annually for twelve measures), and mitigation potentials (31%-33% with twelve measures).This underscores that uncertainty stemming from underlying measure assumptions in MACC analyses is substantial, leading to markedly different outcomes communicated to policymakers. It further highlights the critical importance of transparency regarding underlying assumptions and data. Overall, cost uncertainty exceeds that of mitigation effects. Some measures exhibit zero or negative costs, suggesting that barriers beyond economic factors hinder their uptake.

reference: Working Paper series of the Faculty of Economics and Business Administration of Ghent University (No. 25/1125)
title: Effectiveness of a Soft LTV Limit
affiliations: Ghent University - Department of Economics and Ghent University - Department of Financial Economics

detail.title: Effectiveness of a Soft LTV Limit

declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Fonds voor Wetenschappelijk Onderzoek (FWO), grant number FWO.OPR.2023.0054.01.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Working Paper series of the Faculty of Economics and Business Administration of Ghent University (No. 25/1125)

detail.abstract: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of a soft Loan-to-Value (LTV) limit as a borrower-based macroprudential tool. Our analysis is based on detailed loan-level data from a major Belgian bank, covering all new mortgage originations between 2016 and 2021. Using the 2020 Belgian LTV recommendations as a quasi-natural experiment, we analyze how a non-binding framework that allows tolerance margins affects mortgage lending behavior. We develop a hybrid approach combining machine-learning (ML) predictions of counterfactual treatment status with a difference-indifferences (DiD) and triple-differences (DDD) design. The ML model, trained on pre-policy data, identifies borrowers likely to exceed the 90% LTV threshold in absence of the reform, allowing consistent treatment classification across periods. Our results show that the introduction of a soft LTV limit leads to a significant decline in average LTV ratios and in the share of high-LTV loans (higher than 90%), with stronger effects among constrained borrowers. The adjustment occurs gradually, reflecting banks' progressive adaptation to supervisory expectations rather than abrupt credit rationing. The reduction in leverage is primarily achieved through higher down payments, which leads to lower monthly repayments and thus lower credit risk. When focusing on the exceptions we find convincing evidence that banks especially favor first-time-buyers, since they remain significantly more present in the above 90% mortgage segment compared to non-FTB. Differences in age, savings, and income also lead to differentiated treatment effects, indicating that banks apply the soft limits in a risk-sensitive and targeted manner. These findings demonstrate that soft borrower-based measures can achieve prudential objectives similar to hard caps without exacerbating credit exclusion. From a policy perspective, the Belgian experience highlights that supervisory guidance can effectively curb excessive leverage while maintaining mortgage accessibility.

title: Does FDI Accelerate Global Economic Fragmentation under Geopolitical Tensions?
affiliations: Central University of Finance and Economics, Central University of Finance and Economics and Central University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Does FDI Accelerate Global Economic Fragmentation under Geopolitical Tensions?
detail.abstract: Geopolitical uncertainties are reshaping global foreign direct investment (FDI) patterns, diverting flows toward politically aligned countries and reflecting a deepening global economic fragmentation. Using bilateral data for 38 economies from 2005 to 2023 within a structural equation modeling framework, this study examines the role of FDI in business cycle co-movement. The results indicate that FDI significantly strengthens synchronization, primarily through cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&A). Disaggregating 20 two-digit ISIC industries reveals that intra-industry M&As enhance co-movement, whereas cross-industry M&As weaken it. Furthermore, closer political relations amplify this synchronizing effect of FDI at both the country and industry levels. Overall, the findings demonstrate that amid rising geopolitical tensions, FDI has become a key channel through which political alignment shapes economic interdependence, thereby reinforcing global fragmentation.

title: The Risk–Proportionality Option Pricing: An Exact Division-Form Extension of the Sharpe–Consistency Framework

detail.title: The Risk–Proportionality Option Pricing: An Exact Division-Form Extension of the Sharpe–Consistency Framework
detail.abstract: This paper extends the Sharpe-Consistency Pricing (SCP) framework to incorporate the Risk–Proportionality Principle (RPP), producing an exact division-form equilibrium for real-world option valuation. Under RPP, expected excess returns are proportional rather than equal, with efficiency coefficient ϕ < 1 capturing Sharpe-ratio degradation due to frictions or behavioral asymmetries. Embedding this proportional structure within the SCP normalization yields the exact ϕ-adjusted Sharpe-Consistency identity. The resulting closed-form call and put premium equations operate directly under the physical measure, preserving full Sharpe consistency without PDEs or risk-neutral transformations. The classical SCP and Black–Scholes–Merton (BSM) results appear as limiting cases when ϕ = 1.

title: The Influence of Unilateral Environmental Taxes on Firms’ Internationalisation Decisions
affiliations: University of Valencia and University of Valencia

detail.title: The Influence of Unilateral Environmental Taxes on Firms’ Internationalisation Decisions
detail.abstract: We analyse the extent to which strategic, unilateral environmental policy influences market structure when firms decide strategically how to supply the foreign market, either through exports or foreign direct investment. In a sequential setting, the taxing government must anticipate that firms may find it profitable to change their internationalisation decisions, resulting in lower welfare; this means that, in equilibrium, the government may not be able to implement the welfare maximising tax. We show that, in most cases, the government can induce the market outcome that yields the highest possible welfare, which may not coincide with the resulting market structure in the absence of the environmental tax, therefore influencing the location choice of firms. Besides, for relatively high setupcosts and high enough marginal environmental damages, the government cannot change her firm’s decision and shift it from exports to FDI.

title: Quota Regulation under Corruption -- Grand, Petty and the Cut-Money Culture
affiliations: Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research and Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research

detail.title: Quota Regulation under Corruption -- Grand, Petty and the Cut-Money Culture
detail.abstract: This paper examines the implications of different forms of corruption, i.e., grand corruption, petty corruption, and cut-money culture, on the formulation and enforcement of regulatory policies. Focusing on quota regulation in the context of natural resource extraction, it demonstrates the following. In the absence of cut-money culture, petty corruption never occurs in equilibrium, irrespective of whether the policymaker is honest or corrupt. However, when the policymaker is corrupt, the threat of petty corruption leaves no room for grand corruption, unless environmental damage due to extraction is sufficiently discounted, in which case grand corruption occurs. In contrast, the presence of cut-money culture induces corruption, either petty or both grand and petty, in equilibrium. Cut-money culture may reduce the equilibrium quota from the `no petty corruption enforcing quota', however, whenever this occurs, total extraction and environmental damage rise, and welfare declines. Our results have important implications for designing corruption control mechanisms and governing natural resource extraction.

title: Digital Public Infrastructure and Agricultural Modernization: Causal Evidence from “Broadband China” Policy
affiliations: Qingdao Agricultural University, Qingdao Agricultural University and Qingdao Agricultural University

detail.title: Digital Public Infrastructure and Agricultural Modernization: Causal Evidence from “Broadband China” Policy
detail.abstract: Digital public infrastructure has become a critical enabler of inclusive development, offering new opportunities for transforming agricultural systems in developing economies. This study employs panel data from 300 cities at and above the prefecture level in China between 2007 and 2023, treating the “Broadband China” policy as a quasi-natural experiment. It empirically examines the impact and underlying mechanisms of digital public infrastructure on agricultural modernization. The findings reveal: (1) The “Broadband China” policy significantly accelerates agricultural modernization. (2) The policy promotes modernization primarily by enhancing agricultural technological innovation and strengthening economic agglomeration. (3) Heterogeneity analyses further reveal that policy effects are stronger in cities with more developed logistics systems and lower information search costs. This study contributes new causal evidence on the development impacts of digital public infrastructure and provides policy implications for advancing rural digital inclusion and agricultural transformation in China and other developing economies.

title: Rethinking (In)formalities in Urban Global South Mobilities
affiliations: and

detail.title: Rethinking (In)formalities in Urban Global South Mobilities
detail.abstract: As Global South cities grow, gaps in government-provided services persist along with diverse privately-produced solutions. Fundamental to the support of precarious livelihoods and functioning of urban ecosystems, these privately produced services are often deemed “informal” and excluded from government planning, policies and funding. Services, such as housing and street vending ⎯and their associated informalities⎯ have been the subject of substantial theorization. However, what is often called “informal” mobility tends to be less scrutinized within critical urban informality theory. To explore this potential gap, we carried out two separate literature reviews, one on Global South urban informality and another on “informal” mobility. We asked: are these bodies of scholarship engaging with one another and if so, how? How might they work together to provide deeper insights into informalities and their workings? Overall, we find that both bodies of knowledge remain siloed; this is a missed opportunity. Critical urban informality theories, frameworks and methods might aid in better understanding informalities in mobilities; these mobility services might also serve as a fertile ground to empirically test critical urban informality theories. Besides providing an overview of the evolution of the mobility scholarship and conceptualization of informalities within it, this paper reinforces the need for more research that theorizes and unpacks overly simplistic formal/informal dichotomies within mobility studies, often constructed and used as a marginalization mechanism. We recommend disaggregating different categories of informalities, exploring how informalities are produced and studying the synergies and interrelations with diverse services as assemblages in which mobility services are embedded.

title: Applying the FDMM: Reconstructing Moden War

detail.title: Applying the FDMM: Reconstructing Moden War
detail.abstract:
This paper examines how the Fractal Dynamic Decision-Making Model (FDMM), introduced in the previous paper, can be applied to real domains of life—namely decision-making, conflict, and war.

Each section analyzes one of these domains, thereby clarifying how the model functions under different conditions of purpose, means, and uncertainty.

Section 2 applies the FDMM to corporate competition, showing that business strategy follows the same war-logic: all actions ultimately aim at collapsing the opponent’s will to compete.
This reveals why a firm must align every method—direct or indirect—to its highest purpose, just as in war.

Section 3 analyzes how the flaws in Clausewitz’s original Trinity—flaws that prevent it from coherently explaining modern warfare—can be identified and resolved through a reconstructed formulation.

Section 4 integrates the theories of Clausewitz and Sun Tzu into the FDMM framework, demonstrating how both traditions converge within a unified model of decision-making 

This reconstructed Trinity is then shown to provide clear explanatory power for irregular warfare, including cases of partisan resistance, guerrilla movements, and culturally driven conflicts.

publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We evaluate the effect of California's 11 percent excise tax on firearms, introduced in July 2024, on retail prices. Using price quotes for 48 popular firearms from over 2,200 licensed dealers, we compare California prices to those in other states and to pre-tax trends. We find that prices in California increase by about 10% in response to the 11% tax. Results are consistent across gun types and show no evidence of border spillovers. These findings indicate that firearm excise taxes can effectively raise consumer prices.

title: Learning to Work Towards Goals: A Sequential Evaluation of the Effect of a Goal-Setting Course on Academic and Soft Skills
affiliations: University of Oxford, University of Chicago, University of Chicago, Wageningen University and Utrecht University

detail.title: Learning to Work Towards Goals: A Sequential Evaluation of the Effect of a Goal-Setting Course on Academic and Soft Skills

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-146
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: This study sequentially evaluates a soft-skills course implemented in Ugandan and Kenyan primary schools that replaced academic review time with lessons on goal-setting and related skills as students prepared for high-stakes primary school-leaving exams. An exploratory evaluation in Uganda provided evidence of positive impacts on girls' test scores. A confirmatory evaluation in Kenya found that the course led to improvements in self-reported soft skills, especially among girls, although no gains in test scores. The study illustrates the utility of sequential evaluation, with exploratory analysis to identify promising hypotheses, followed by out-of-sample testing, as a tool to uncover heterogeneous effects.

title: Bank Liquidity Management and Payout Policy under Peer Pressure
affiliations: Florida International University, Florida International University (FIU) and Getulio Vargas Foundation (FGV) - EMAp - School of Applied Mathematics

detail.title: Bank Liquidity Management and Payout Policy under Peer Pressure
detail.abstract: We study how peer effects in liquidity management influence banks’ payout decisions and systemic risk. We develop a dynamic model in which banks choose dividends to maximize shareholder value while facing adjustment costs and peer pressure that penalize deviations from industry-average liquid reserves. The model predicts nonlinear, state-dependent payout responses that are strongly influenced by peer pressure. Using the Federal Reserve Y-9C data from 1987–2020, we confirm the model’s prediction that payouts increase with liquidity levels and reserve deviations. Additionally, low-liquidity banks reduce payouts under peer pressure, while high-liquidity banks increase them. Stronger peer pressure elevates default risk, amplifying payout heterogeneity and raising concerns about systemic financial vulnerability.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-150
title: Who Chooses and Who Benefits? The Design of Public School Choice Systems
affiliations: University of Chicago Booth School of Business, University of Texas at Austin, Brown University and University of Texas at Austin

detail.title: Who Chooses and Who Benefits? The Design of Public School Choice Systems

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-150
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: Public school choice has evolved rapidly in the past two decades, as districts roll out new magnet, dual-language, and themed programs to broaden educational opportunity. We use newly collected national data to document that opt-in (voluntary) systems: (i) are the modal design; (ii) are harder to navigate; and (iii) have participation that is concentrated among more advantaged students. These facts suggest a striking inconsistency: districts have largely adopted centralized assignment algorithms to broaden access, but most rely on optional participation that fragments public education. We study the implications of this design choice in the Los Angeles Unified School District, the largest opt-in system in the country, combining nearly two decades of administrative data, randomized lotteries, and quasi-experimental expansions in access. Participation is highly selective, consistent with national evidence, and lottery estimates suggest that the students with the lowest demand for choice schools are the ones who gain the most from attending. Opt-in participation therefore embeds a selection mechanism that screens out high-return students and leaves many effective programs with unused capacity. To evaluate system-level implications, we estimate a structural model linking applications, enrollment, and achievement. Choice schools are vertically differentiated and generate meaningful gains, but the opt-in participation rule-through high application costs and negative selection on gains-prevents these benefits from reaching the students who need them most. Counterfactual simulations make the design stakes clear: information and travel-cost reductions have limited effects, whereas reforms that change the participation architecture eliminate core inefficiencies and deliver the largest district-wide achievement gains. These results underscore that system designnot school effectiveness alone-shapes who benefits from public school choice and to what extent.

reference: Washington Journal of Law & Policy, forthcoming 2026
title: The Governance of Clinical Trial Data

detail.title: The Governance of Clinical Trial Data

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Washington Journal of Law & Policy, forthcoming 2026

detail.abstract:
Clinical trial results are among the most authoritative inputs in biomedical research and are increasingly reused as training, calibration, and evaluation data for AI systems. Yet a large share of completed trials, especially small academic studies, pilot projects, and early-phase experiments, never disclose their findings. These omissions distort meta-analyses, hide negative results, and silently propagate upstream bias into AI models. Existing enforcement tools, including FDA civil penalties and NIH grant sanctions, work tolerably well for high-stakes commercial trials when used, but fail across the long tail, where investigators lack the resources or incentives to upload results once grant funds expire. 

This Article reframes clinical-trial transparency as a training-data governance problem and proposes a complementary solution: modest fixed cost-offsets for compliant uploads, funded through a two-tier access model. Public summaries on ClinicalTrials.gov would remain free, while a licensed API would provide harmonized, machine-readable datasets to high-volume users such as insurers, pharmaceutical consortia, and AI developers. Aligning the distribution of costs and benefits makes transparency feasible for resource-constrained investigators and sustainable for the analytic institutions that depend on complete, unbiased data. The result is a light-touch institutional architecture that preserves fragile trial evidence and strengthens the reliability of both biomedical research and AI health systems.

title: Fragmented Teams and the Hidden Dynamics of Organisational Misalignment: A Conceptual Model for Identifying and Addressing Sub-Team Behaviour

detail.title: Fragmented Teams and the Hidden Dynamics of Organisational Misalignment: A Conceptual Model for Identifying and Addressing Sub-Team Behaviour
detail.abstract: Teams inside organisations often appear cohesive and functional, yet beneath the surface they may fragment into sub-teams with distinct norms, loyalties, and behavioural patterns. This conceptual paper examines how such fragmentation emerges and stabilises, particularly in multi-site organisations where centralised headquarters and decentralised field units operate under different structural and contextual conditions. Adopting a conceptual approach, the paper brings together research on mechanistic and organic structures (Burns and Stalker, 1961), group faultlines (Bezrukova et al., 2012), organisational silence (Morrison and Milliken, 2000), psychological safety, leadership dynamics, and sub-cultures. These streams contributions are synthesised into a multi-domain framework that explains how sub-team behaviour forms, stabilises, and creates alignment risks across sites. Fragmentation typically develops gradually through everyday adaptations, workarounds, and selective communication rather than through dramatic failures. The paper proposes a five-domain conceptual model that explains how sub-team behaviour is shaped by the interaction of structural design, leadership and leadingship behaviour, communication and information flows, behavioural climate, and work and reward systems. The model is intended as a diagnostic lens for senior managers, consultants, and organisational practitioners to identify early warning signs of misalignment before trust, cohesion, knowledge sharing, and performance deteriorate. By integrating structural and micro-behavioural perspectives, the paper contributes to a more systemic understanding of fragmentation and highlights opportunities for future empirical research on how behavioural drift emerges, spreads, and becomes normalised across organisational settings.

reference: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-149
title: Africa as a Success Story: Political Organization in Pre-Colonial Africa
affiliations: and University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy

detail.title: Africa as a Success Story: Political Organization in Pre-Colonial Africa

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-149
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We provide an overview of the explanations for the relative lack of state formation historically in Africa. In doing so we systematically document for the first time the extent to which Africa was politically decentralized, calculating that in 1880 there were probably 45,000 independent polities which were rarely organized on ethnic lines. At most 2% of these could be classified as states. We advance a new argument for this extreme political decentralization positing that African societies were deliberately organized to stop centralization emerging. In this they were successful. We point out some key aspects of African societies that helped them to manage this equilibrium. We also emphasize how the organization of the economy was subservient to these political goals.

title: Measurement Matters: Financial Reporting and Productivity
affiliations: Yale School of Management, U.S. Census Bureau, Boston University - Questrom School of Business and University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Measurement Matters: Financial Reporting and Productivity

publicationDetails.detailsText: University of Chicago, Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper No. 2025-148
publicationDetails.journalName: Becker Friedman Institute for Economics Working Paper Series

detail.abstract: We examine how differences in financial reporting practices shape firm productivity. Leveraging new audit questions in the U.S. Census Bureau's 2021 Management and Organizational Practices Survey (MOPS), and complementary tax return data from the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and detailed financial records from Sageworks, we find that (i) variation in reporting quality explains 10-20 percent of intra-industry total factor productivity dispersion, and (ii) evidence of complementarity between the effects of financial audits and management practices driving firm productivity. We then examine the underlying mechanisms. First, audits function as a managerial technology, improving the precision of internal information and raising efficiency, with stronger effects in competitive, low-margin industries and among younger firms. Second, exploiting crossstate variation in tax incentives, we show that audits constrain underreporting and mitigate the downward bias in measured productivity. Together, these results highlight the underrated importance of financial reporting quality driving firm productivity.

title: Influence of Interventions on Building Practitioners' Beyond-Compliance with Residential Energy Performance Standards
affiliations: Deakin University, Deakin University and Deakin University

detail.title: Influence of Interventions on Building Practitioners' Beyond-Compliance with Residential Energy Performance Standards
detail.abstract: Building practitioners often fail to achieve beyond-compliance with residential energy performance standards, jeopardizing industry sustainability. Governments increasingly employ policies to drive behaviour change towards beyond-compliance. However, the influence of interventions on building practitioners' compliance behaviour remains under-explored, along with the consideration of social interactions among these practitioners. This study aims to assess the influence of interventions on building practitioners' beyond-compliance in Australia. Two specific objectives are set accordingly: To identify the specific behavioural constructs impacted by interventions; and to evaluate the extent of behaviour change resulting from interventions, particularly in achieving better beyond-compliance outcomes. Data was gathered from a survey of 73 building practitioners involved in residential design, including architects, designers, builders, project managers, and thermal performance assessors. Agent-Based Modelling was used to simulate behaviour changes compared to initial self-reported behaviour states under the influence of two widely implemented policies: training and financial incentive. The findings show that while training improves knowledge of energy-efficient designs, it does not lead to tangible improvements in achieving beyond-compliance outcomes. Conversely, financial incentive effectively drives behaviour change in delivering homes that are beyond-compliance by offsetting perceived high compliance costs. These results provide valuable insights for policymakers and industry advisory bodies, enabling them to develop more targeted interventions that align with building practitioners' interests, ultimately contributing to the sustainability of the residential building sector.

title: The Economics of Not Knowing: A Symmetric Ignorance Theory of IPO Pricing
affiliations: University of Zurich and Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR), Swedish House of Finance

detail.title: The Economics of Not Knowing: A Symmetric Ignorance Theory of IPO Pricing

declarations.funderStatement: Ljungqvist gratefully acknowledges generous funding from the Knut & Alice Wallenberg Foundation (grant no. KAW 2023.0270)

detail.abstract: We develop a unified framework in which IPO practices operate not to manage asymmetric information but to prevent it from arising. Costly information acquisition gives investors an option to pick and choose among offerings, forcing the underwriter to offer a discount. IPO practices lower the value of this option-by diminishing the quality, relevance, or payoff of investor information-and thereby reduce the discount required to deter information production. This information-prevention perspective offers a coherent explanation for otherwise disparate practices, resolves persistent empirical puzzles about IPO allocations, and yields new implications for cornerstone investors and the JOBS Act.

title: Positional Rules, the Pairwise-Majority-Loser, and Single-Peaked Preferences
affiliations: Kansai University - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Positional Rules, the Pairwise-Majority-Loser, and Single-Peaked Preferences
detail.abstract: We investigate the pairwise-majority-loser consistency of positional rules on the single-peaked preference domain. Pairwise-majority-loser consistency requires that a voting rule never selects the pairwise-majority-loser as a winner. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition under which a positional rule satisfies this consistency on the single-peaked preference domain. This condition concerns either the number of ranks assigned a score of 1, with scores normalized such that the highest-ranked alternative receives a score of 1, or the scores of two ranks symmetrically positioned around the median rank. Our theorem demonstrates that restricting the domain to single-peaked preferences substantially enlarges the class of positional rules that satisfy pairwise-majority-loser consistency, whereas on the unrestricted preference domain, only the Borda rule satisfies this property (Fishburn and Gehrlein, 1976; Okamoto and Sakai, 2019).

reference: Accepted for publication for CRIOCM 29th (2024) International Symposium
title: Causes for Minimal Compliance in Residential Building Energy Performance Standards
affiliations: Deakin University, Deakin University and Deakin University

detail.title: Causes for Minimal Compliance in Residential Building Energy Performance Standards

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted for publication for CRIOCM 29th (2024) International Symposium

detail.abstract: Minimal compliance with the energy performance standards for residential buildings is a common issue. The study aims to comprehensively investigate the causes for minimal compliance relating to energy performance standards in the residential building industry. A systematic literature review applying a three-step review method in Scopus and Web of Science has identified 25 articles. Through thematic analysis, 10 causes were identified and categorized into two themes: technical causes and human-related causes. Regarding the frequency of the causes mentioned, 47% of the causes reported on the technical dimension. 53% reported on the human dimension, in particular, 15% related to building end-users and 38% related to building practitioners. Furthermore, an in-depth investigation of the causes through correlation analysis highlighted the influence mechanisms of the causes. Especially, the flawed energy performance assessment model may generate results which didn't match reality, leading to overestimating energy consumption and failing to meet compliance standards. Moreover, a short familiarization period with insufficient capacity building resources might leave the industry unprepared, decreasing their ability to achieve higher compliance outcome. Additionally, building end-users usually worry about high cost of energy-efficient homes, potentially reducing demand for houses exceeding minimum requirements. This research raises awareness among policymakers and relevant stakeholders (e.g., building practitioners or industry organisations who advance residential building energy efficiency) in providing a better understanding of the issues of minimal compliance in residential building energy performance standards.

title:
Allied Commitments and Public Support for Military Interventions
A Cross-National Experiment
affiliations: Charles University , Charles University in Prague and Charles University in Prague

detail.title:
Allied Commitments and Public Support for Military Interventions
A Cross-National Experiment
detail.abstract: Recent survey experiments have found that the public in NATO countries is more supportive of intervening militarily on behalf of formal allies than non-allies. However, we lack empirical evidence on whether this effect of alliance treaties generalizes to non-NATO and non-Western publics. To fill this gap, we conducted a preregistered cross-national survey experiment on population samples (N = 7,200) in two Western NATO countries (the United States and the United Kingdom) and four non-Western regional powers (Russia, China, India, and Brazil). We show that while allied commitments shaped public support for military interventions in the pooled cross-national sample, their effect was significantly weaker in non-Western, non-NATO countries. Using a mediation analysis, we also found that feelings of moral obligation and the concerns about the reputational costs of non-intervention were similarly important mechanisms linking alliances to public support for honoring defense commitments. Our findings contribute to the scholarly debates on the microfoundations of collective defense and the generalizability of IR experiments beyond the Western context.

title: Cultural Narcissism as a Universal Developmental Failure Mode: Humility as the Gate to Prosocial Transmission and Well-Being

detail.title: Cultural Narcissism as a Universal Developmental Failure Mode: Humility as the Gate to Prosocial Transmission and Well-Being
detail.abstract: Cultural Narcissism (CN) is a developmentally normative, population-wide condition, not a marginal pathology. Across approximately 36 behavioral and informant-based studies (aggregate N ≈ 18,500), spanning at least 12 countries, CN shows a consistent and damaging signature: prosocial behavior is inflated under visibility by approximately 10-12 percentage points relative to anonymous conditions (public vs. anonymous Hedges' g ≈ 0.28, 95% CI [0.20, 0.36]) while collapsing under anonymity, cost, error exposure, and temporal persistence. Meta-analytic structural equation models demonstrate that this divergence is systemic, not situational. When humility-indexed behaviors-error admission, non-defensive self-assessment, tolerance of anonymity-are absent, associations among honesty, compassion, responsibility, and courage collapse to near zero, and no reliable pathway to eudaimonic well-being remains (r ≈ .00-.05). Prior work on the Progression of Virtues showed that only prosocial behavior surviving these constraints compounds into durable well-being (r ≈ .32-.38; Hawkins, 2025). Without humility, human development defaults to performance, not transformation.

title: Pre-Grant Patents and Innovation Diffusion

detail.title: Pre-Grant Patents and Innovation Diffusion
detail.abstract: Are pre-grant patents effective forward-looking signals of global innovation diffusion? Patent grants are important legal milestones, but information diffusion about the underlying technologies occurs at the time patents are published. As the innovation literature rarely studies this distinction, I address this question using pre-grant patent flows across countries, sectors, and industries over time. This allows me to separately identify timing effects on diffusion and those that are running through either innovation or trade channels. At country level, results show that the innovation channel creates larger and more persistent total factor productivity (TFP) gains and stock price responses. This confirms that international technology spillovers originate from the expansion of the global stock of knowledge rather than strategic changes in trade intensity between home countries and their partners. A one-standard-deviation foreign pre-grant patent shock raises manufacturing-sector TFP by about 1.5%, and the R&D capital stock rises by roughly 0.4% with a one-year delay. This reflects their forward-looking nature, which prompts resource reallocation in anticipation of future productivity gains. These gains are especially pronounced in countries which manufacturing sectors that are more R&D-intensive. At the industry level, the results show that countries with more value-added-intensive industries are better able to translate pre-grant patents citations into higher labour productivity gains.

detail.abstract: This article introduces Hierarchical Core-Orbital Allocation (HCOA), a portfolio construction framework that decouples the statistical structure of clustering from economic optimization through a two-level architecture. At the strategic level, representative "core" assets are selected within homogeneous clusters and optimized using any objective function-minimum variance, maximum Sharpe, or risk parity. At the tactical level, these weights are redistributed to "orbital" assets while preserving hierarchical coherence: intra-cluster allocations exactly reproduce upper-level decisions. This design offers three properties: numerical robustness through dimensionality reduction, functional flexibility across objective combinations, and structural coherence linking both allocation tiers. Applied to USD-denominated bonds spanning sovereign, supranational, and corporate credit categories, HCOA demonstrates how clustering can serve portfolio construction without constraining optimization methodology. The framework reproduces the inherent hierarchy of fixed-income markets: cores capture systematic factors while orbitals preserve instrument-level diversification. HCOA provides an adaptive architecture that separates what clustering does well from what optimization must decide.

title: The Scholar Who Noticed the Stitch: Life and Work of Mira Sinha Bhattacharjea

detail.abstract: This memorial essay traces the intellectual trajectory and legacy of Mira Sinha Bhattacharjea (1930-2009), a pioneering scholar who transitioned from diplomacy to academia to establish the foundations of Chinese studies in India. The narrative follows her early resistance to domestic constraints and her entry into the Indian Foreign Service in the 1950s, where she navigated a male-dominated institution to specialize in the Chinese language. Her subsequent posting in Beijing revealed a society characterized by collective discipline and a focus on basic human needs, offering a perspective that contrasted sharply with later geopolitical narratives. Following the 1962 Sino-Indian War and the resulting diplomatic deterioration, Bhattacharjea resigned from government service to seek intellectual autonomy. The essay details her critical role in forming the Institute of Chinese Studies, initially an informal gathering known as the "Wednesday Group", where she sought to create a space for "unlearning" biases and challenging Cold War frameworks during periods of high anti-China sentiment. Her scholarship argued that India and China must be studied as civilizations with long memories rather than through Western political lenses or reactionary nationalism. Ultimately, the essay presents Bhattacharjea's life as an embodiment of an "ethic of attention", suggesting that the patient, humble study of a rival power is a source of strategic strength.

detail.abstract: The paper "How do social, legal and economic factors influence women's empowerment in Bangladesh and other developing countries?" tries to make an analytical comparison from its theoretical and empirical status. It reiterates the imperatives of women's empowerment as integral to society and economic development objectives, guaranteeing gender equality, economic growth, and social justice for developing countries. The paper is dominated by the high complexity of the challenge of empowering women within the socio-cultural, legal, and economic context of countries as diverse as Bangladesh. The paper alludes to the diverse patriarchal roles that are traditional and only seem to restrict women's visibility in public and private spheres; they go ahead to outline the major stumbling block that women seem to face, which includes discrimination, abuse, and the lack of access to resources. However, the visibility of women, especially in the various professional fields, is slowly but steadily increasing, a progress towards a vision of gender equality. Using data from 124 countries, the paper establishes a connection between continuous disempowerment and the invisibility of leadership positions for women alongside a patriarchal culture. Further exploration is done about globalization and how it has affected empowering women in terms of economic participation and cultural transformation, pointing out the opportunities and risks involved. The paper also explores the legal environment of Bangladesh, which still lags not only in protecting but also in enforcing the rights of women, despite some legislative attempts. The cross-country comparative analysis of this research will go a long way toward drawing the lines within which different influencing factors interplay to the empowerment of women in developing countries. In this respect, it shall also come up with common challenges and promising practices that can guide policy and advocacy. The paper ultimately emphasizes the need for comprehensive approaches that consider socioeconomic and legal factors to remove barriers, thereby promoting conditions in which women can be a core component of societal progress.

title: The Influence of Unilateral Environmental Taxes on Firms’ Internationalisation Decisions
affiliations: University of Valencia and University of Valencia

detail.title: The Influence of Unilateral Environmental Taxes on Firms’ Internationalisation Decisions
detail.abstract: We analyse the extent to which strategic, unilateral environmental policy influences market structure when firms decide strategically how to supply the foreign market, either through exports or foreign direct investment. In a sequential setting, the taxing government must anticipate that firms may find it profitable to change their internationalisation decisions, resulting in lower welfare; this means that, in equilibrium, the government may not be able to implement the welfare maximising tax. We show that, in most cases, the government can induce the market outcome that yields the highest possible welfare, which may not coincide with the resulting market structure in the absence of the environmental tax, therefore influencing the location choice of firms. Besides, for relatively high setupcosts and high enough marginal environmental damages, the government cannot change her firm’s decision and shift it from exports to FDI.

title: Housing Inequality in the United States
affiliations: Vanderbilt University - College of Arts and Science - Department of Economics,  and Université Libre de Bruxelles (ULB)
