detail.abstract: We use county assessor and property deed records to construct, analyze, and disseminate contemporaneous and long-run estimates of housing inequality for the United States and its subnational levels. A dwelling in the top decile is eight times as valuable and four times as large as a dwelling in the bottom decile, and 12% of all housing assets are held by 1% of households. Housing value inequality has increased since the 1980s, while housing space inequality has remained relatively stable. Heterogeneity is substantial, with considerable variation between and within states, commuting zones, and census tracts. Income, land-use regulations, and housing supply and demand are associated with current and changing levels of housing inequality. This research highlights the importance of granularity when studying inequality and evaluating policies. We make all estimates publicly available to facilitate such work.

title: As Competition Rises, Do Microfinance Institutions Change Their Lending Practices? Evidence from Panel Data
affiliations: Whitman College and A2F Consulting

detail.title: As Competition Rises, Do Microfinance Institutions Change Their Lending Practices? Evidence from Panel Data
detail.abstract: The microcredit sector has expanded rapidly over the past two decades, giving borrowers more outside options and in theory weakening their repayment incentives. Yet, in practice, repayment rates remain remarkably high. This paper examines how microfinance institutions (MFIs) adjust their contract terms in response to rising competition. Motivated by a simple theoretical framework, we empirically study how for-profit and nonprofit MFIs use two lending contract terms, interest rates and leniency, to preserve repayment incentives. We find that the two types of MFIs respond differently to competition: for-profits lower interest rates but do not significantly adjust their leniency, while nonprofits mainly reduce leniency but keep their interest rates unchanged.

title: MPFNet: Mamba-Driven Progressive Fusion Network for RAW-RGB Collaborative Demoiréing
affiliations: , , ,  and

detail.title: MPFNet: Mamba-Driven Progressive Fusion Network for RAW-RGB Collaborative Demoiréing
detail.abstract: With the development of smartphone and display technologies, screen-captured images have become an indispensable means for recording information. However, moiré patterns, generated due to the aliasing effect between the Color Filter Array (CFA) and screen display pixels, severely degrade image quality. Existing demoiré methods suffer from issues such as significant loss of original information in RGB images, limited receptive field range, and high computational complexity, leading to incomplete removal of moiré patterns. To address these limitations, we propose a Mamba-Driven Progressive Fusion Network (MPFNet) for RAW-RGB Collaborative Demoiréing. The MPFNet fully leverages RAW data (which retains richer original information) and RGB data (which provides guidance during RAW-to-RGB conversion), while harnessing the global receptive field attention enabled by Mamba's linear computational complexity, thereby achieving low-color-difference moiré removal. The MPFNet adopts a two-stage architecture: In the first stage, a Simple Demoiré Block (SDB) performs shallow demoiréing on RAW data while extracting multi-scale RAW features. In the second stage, the dual-path adaptive feature fusion (DAFF) module is used to progressively fuse multi-scale RAW and RGB features, and then the DemoiréMamba Block (DMB) is used to achieve deep moiré removal and accurate color restoration. Extensive experiments on TMM22, RAWVDemoiré and FHDMI datasets demonstrate that MPFNet achieves state-of-the-art performance in both quantitative metrics and qualitative visual comparisons, while maintaining relatively low FLOPs. For instance, MPFNet achieves a PSNR of 28.86 dB on the TMM22 dataset, which is 0.51 dB higher than previous methods, and it also has lower GFLOPs.

title: CO2 footprint of bottom trawling, recognising the value and need to improve marine management
affiliations: , University of Auckland and

detail.title: CO2 footprint of bottom trawling, recognising the value and need to improve marine management
detail.abstract: Bottom trawling is one of the most widespread anthropogenic disturbances to marine sediments and threatens to transform these long-term carbon sinks into sources of CO emissions. The fate of resuspended organic matter remineralized into CO2 remains poorly quantified and its relevance to climate mitigation and marine management largely overlooked. To address this gap, we estimated CO released from sediment disturbance by bottom trawling in the Hauraki Gulf Marine Park, using Global Fishing Watch effort data combined with regionally derived resuspension-induced CO production rates and sediment characteristics. We also examined how these releases align with newly implemented conservation areas and evaluated economic value under different carbon pricing frameworks to assess their potential integration into carbon markets. Our results indicate that bottom trawling releases an average of 2,126 tonnes of CO per year into the water column in the Hauraki Gulf, equivalent to trawling activity releasing 3.12 tCO km² yr¹. These findings identify that bottom trawling represents negative additionality to national carbon budgets and highlight the importance of integrating seafloor carbon sinks into marine spatial planning and fisheries management to support both ecological and carbon storage outcomes. Furthermore, our economic valuation highlights the potential for recognising the carbon sink function of marine sediments within carbon accounting and marine management frameworks.

title: Broadband Internet Access and the Skill Content of Online Vacancies
affiliations: , Catholic University of the Sacred Heart of Milan and Department of Economics and Management

detail.title: Broadband Internet Access and the Skill Content of Online Vacancies
detail.abstract: We investigate the response of posted job vacancies to increased broadband connectivity, with a specific focus on their skill content and conditioning the effects on digital and non-digital occupations. In our large dataset, broadband shocks unambiguously increase vacancy postings but do not significantly impact their digital skill composition. By contrast, fast broadband shocks induce heterogeneous responses, where vacancies posted for non-digital occupations increase their digital/cognitive skill content, whereas we obtain opposite results for digital occupations. We provide a direct quantitative assessment of the changing (digital/cognitive) skill composition of labour demand as a consequence of technological innovations associated with increasing fast broadband connectivity. Our results bear implications for the training of workers in response to (and anticipation of) digitisation.

title: Market Mechanism Design and Trading Decision Model Incorporating Renewable Energy Alliances for the Future Electricity Capacity Market of China
affiliations: North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University, Beijing Institute of Technology, North China Electric Power University, North China Electric Power University,  and

detail.title: Market Mechanism Design and Trading Decision Model Incorporating Renewable Energy Alliances for the Future Electricity Capacity Market of China
detail.abstract: This study extends research by prospectively exploring a capacity market, and proposes a systematic framework for China’s capacity market incorporating multi-timescale dimensions and localized refinements, addressing a critical gap. We develop a multi-strategy capacity trading decision model incorporating carbon emission costs and strategic differences in profit structures. Mathematical derivations validate the model's rationality and elucidate decision conditions and corresponding characteristic application. Case studies demonstrate that current capacity price fails to incentivize adequate capacity support for system reliability unless raised to 2.57 times the existing level, or supplemented by higher spot prices—each 10% spot prices rise corresponds to an average 22.51% reduction in required capacity prices. The dual revenue structure, comprising capacity payments from capacity auctions and energy payments from capacity dispatch response, enhances the financial sustainability of coal-fired units, which is the dominant reliable capacity of China. Furthermore, carbon price drives up capacity prices, with each 10% carbon price rise leading to an average 2.98% increase in capacity price. Bilateral leasing shows strong resilience to price volatility, with coal-fired units receiving capacity price exceeding 4 times the prevailing rate even under bargaining power constraints, significantly incentivizing its contribution to system capacity adequacy. Although variations in net load characteristics can fundamentally alter the relative advantages among strategies, the proposed capacity market mechanism and decision model provide coal-fired units with multiple flexible response strategies to adapt to such changes and maximize their capacity value. The mechanism design and findings can offer valuable insights for the development of China's forward capacity market.

title: Inbound business activities and industrial linkages: Insights from Shanghai using an integrated big–small data approach
affiliations: Tongji University, Tongji University, Tongji University, , Tongji University, Tongji University and Tongji University

detail.title: Inbound business activities and industrial linkages: Insights from Shanghai using an integrated big–small data approach
detail.abstract: Functions of global cities are shaped by and shaping intercity activities. Intercity business exchanges, as a driver of industrial linkages, embody this interaction, yet the ways in which inter-city and intra-city dynamics interact to shape these processes remain insufficiently understood. This study addresses this gap by investigating inbound business activities in Shanghai, a prominent global financial and service hub in China. Employing an integrated approach that combines big data from mobile phone data with small data from ground surveys, we identify inbound business travelers and examine the spatial drivers of their activities. The results show that inbound business travelers account for 36.9% of short-term visitors and reinforce Shanghai’s polycentric urban structure through connections with both proximate and distant high-tier cities. Industrial similarity between Shanghai and source counties exerts a U-shaped effect, with business exchanges more likely to occur between regions that are either highly similar or markedly different. Intercity cooperation is mainly characterized by inter-industry linkages, although intra-industry linkages are also present. Finance, real estate, business services, and IT services emerge as the key sectors underpinning Shanghai’s intercity connectivity. These findings deepen our understanding of the dynamics of intercity business travel and provide insights into regional planning and the governance of global urban systems.

title: Believing in institutions and financial wellbeing in the emergent economies: Micro-level evidence from Romania
affiliations: Babes-Bolyai University - Faculty of Economics and Business Administration and

detail.title: Believing in institutions and financial wellbeing in the emergent economies: Micro-level evidence from Romania
detail.abstract: This study explores the relationship between institutional beliefs and individual wellbeing in Romania, a post-communist country still grappling with inefficient institutions and low, uneven welfare. Using survey data from 477 Romanian citizens, the research investigates how perceptions of governance and market institutions correlate with income levels. Main results indicate that individuals with positive views of public governance tend to have lower incomes, whereas those who hold favorable opinions of market economy institutions generally earn more. Among low-income respondents, financial inclusion and a competition-friendly attitude are associated with higher earnings. Conversely, high-income individuals benefit from trust in private companies and positive attitudes toward privatization. Additionally, trust in the justice system and perceived fairness of taxation are associated with higher wages in the private sector, although beliefs regarding market institutions appear unrelated to public sector wages. These findings hold practical relevance for policymakers, economists, and social researchers seeking to enhance wellbeing in transitional economies.

title: Poor and unequal US counties are more vulnerable to hurricane damage
affiliations: Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK), , Potsdam-Institut für Klimafolgenforschung (PIK) and Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK)

detail.title: Poor and unequal US counties are more vulnerable to hurricane damage
detail.abstract: Hurricanes are the most damaging category of extreme weather events in the US. So far, it is unclear how the vulnerability of physical assets to these storms depends upon subnational income and income inequality. We present an event-based econometric approach that blends spatially and temporally resolved representations of individual hurricanes with spatially resolved asset data. We apply it to 1,585 US-county damage events from 72 storms between 1996 and 2021, recorded in the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Storm Events Database. We find that vulnerability is lower in affected counties with higher average per capita income or lower income inequality. These differences are substantial enough to have influenced observed damages during the study period. We conclude that reducing such vulnerability could be an important benefit of policies aimed at reducing inequality and promoting economic development. This finding is particularly relevant given the projected intensification of hurricane impacts due to global warming.

title: Short sale and climate policy uncertainty

detail.title: Short sale and climate policy uncertainty
detail.abstract: This study examines the impact of climate policy uncertainty (CPU) on short-selling activities. Specifically, we examine the impact of CPU index (Gavriilidis (2021)) on stock short interest ratio (SIR). Using a comprehensive U.S. dataset from 2006 to 2018, we find that SIR is positively correlated with CPU, suggesting that short sellers increase their positions in response to higher CPU index, particularly in firms with high institutional ownership, lower liquidity, higher volatility, and greater opinion dispersion. Furthermore, we find that CPU widens pricing discrepancies between stocks and bonds within the same firms. These findings underscore the importance of CPU in influencing financial market behavior, firm valuation, and cross-asset pricing dynamics.

title: Why on-the-Run Treasuries Command a Liquidity Premium
affiliations: GPG College No 1, Abbottabad

detail.title: Why on-the-Run Treasuries Command a Liquidity Premium
detail.abstract: The most recently issued (on-the-run) U.S. Treasury securities consistently trade at slightly higher prices (lower yields) than older, comparable (off-the-run) issues-a persistent liquidity premium or "specialness." This premium reflects the unique market structure of Treasuries and frictions in trading and funding. On-the-run bonds are scarce but highly liquid benchmarks: they are heavily traded on centralized platforms, widely used as collateral, and preferred in risk-hedging strategies, while off-the-run bonds trade infrequently in decentralized dealer markets. We show that market-making dynamics-including dealer inventories, trading volumes, and repo financing-systematically make on-the-run issues more desirable. This drives a convenience yield that links to broader macro themes: on-run Treasuries serve as high-quality collateral in funding markets (repo, reverse repo, central bank operations) and influence monetary policy transmission. Historical stress episodes amplify these patterns: during the 2008-09 crisis, March 2020 turmoil, and recent quantitative-tightening periods, on-run premia spiked as off-run liquidity dried up. We provide a detailed, data-informed analysis of these forces and their implications for the Treasury market and policy.

title: The Inequity of Consumption-Based Tax Systems
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: The Inequity of Consumption-Based Tax Systems
detail.abstract: This study examines the lack of redistributive effectiveness of consumption-based tax systems with respect to social fairness. Through numerical simulations, we explore the wealth exchanges among economic agents subject to flat consumption taxes, comparing universal redistribution with optimal targeted approaches. The results demonstrate that consumption taxes exhibit inherent regressivity, disproportionately burdening the poorest 40% of households who contribute over half of total tax revenue for most tax rates. The findings challenge the equity of consumption taxes and provide quantitative insights for designing more fair fiscal policies.

title: Tackling Greenwashing and Market Imbalance: The Design of a Differentiated Green Electricity Certificate Issuance Mechanism
affiliations: State Grid Shanghai Municipal Electric Power Company, State Grid Shanghai Municipal Electric Power Company and Wuhan  University

detail.title: Tackling Greenwashing and Market Imbalance: The Design of a Differentiated Green Electricity Certificate Issuance Mechanism
detail.abstract: The current homogenized issuance mechanism of "one certificate per MWh" is the structural root cause of the supply-demand imbalance in the green certificate market and the prevalent risk of corporate greenwashing. This paper constructs a differentiated issuance framework based on the dual dimensions of "technical characteristics and market value." By introducing a Data Envelopment Analysis (DEA) model that incorporates technological heterogeneity, we quantify the comprehensive contribution efficiency of nine renewable energy technologies to the "energy impossible triad," thereby enabling a differentiated certificate allocation. Empirical results show that, compared to the traditional mechanism, the differentiated approach can reduce the total annual certificate issuance by approximately 55% from 2025 to 2030. Simultaneously, it enhances the carbon reduction effect per certificate by 72% to 81% and is projected to reverse the supply-demand relationship around 2030. If linked with carbon pricing, the price of a differentiated green certificate is expected to reach 90 Chinese Yuan by 2030, effectively curbing greenwashing incentives. Based on these findings, we propose policy pathways such as dynamic issuance, attribute labeling, and carbon price linkage. This study provides a theoretical foundation and policy tools for reconstructing the value system of green certificates and balancing the economic-security-environmental dimensions of the energy transition.

title: Green product co-design within cheap-talk information disclosure in a supply chain
affiliations: Tianjin University of Technology, Independent and Lanzhou University

detail.title: Green product co-design within cheap-talk information disclosure in a supply chain
detail.abstract: Green product co-design in supply chains has become an important practice, with information disclosure serving as a key facilitator for collaboration. However. the effectiveness of information disclosure, which may involve cheap talk (unverified information), on the collaboration of the supply chain remains unclear. Therefore, this study develop a game-theoretic model to investigate the strategic role of cheap talk in green product co-design, where the supplier determines and discloses its green design strategy, which may involve cheap talk, and the manufacturer subsequently sets its green design strategy based on the received information. Our analysis derives the optimal information disclosure strategy for the supplier and the optimal green design strategies for both parties. We identify two behavioral patterns that cheap talk can induce in the manufacturer: free-riding on the supplier's green efforts and over-investing as a response to the suppliers strategically designed disclosure of low greenness. Importantly, our findings reveal that false disclosure can benefit both parties under certain conditions. By strategically selecting its disclosure strategy, the supplier can influence the manufacturer's design decisions, motivating enhanced greenness. Furthermore, we demonstrate that strategic cheap talk can simultaneously improve both profitability and environmental performance in green supply chain.

title: Legislation and Practice of SPC in EU and Switzerland

detail.title: Legislation and Practice of SPC in EU and Switzerland
detail.abstract: Supplementary protection certificates (SPCs) are an intellectual property right that serve as an extension to a patent right. They apply to specific pharmaceutical and plant protection products that have been authorised by regulatory authorities and aim to offset the loss of patent protection for these products that occurs due to lengthy compulsory testing and clinical trials these products require prior to obtaining regulatory market approval. 1 This article will analyse and compare the legislation and practice of SPCs in the EU and Switzerland, mention relevant court cases and future developments of the matter. 1. EU legislation on SPCs The regulations below provide the legal EU framework for the creation of SPCs for patented pharmaceutical and plant protection products.

title: Reservoir modification - reducing pore pressure to assist in increasing CBM recovery and in-situ disaster gas reduction: Insights from a micro perspective
affiliations: , China University of Mining and Technology-Beijing, , , , , , University of Wollongong, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Institute of Coal Chemistry and Chongqing University

detail.title: Reservoir modification - reducing pore pressure to assist in increasing CBM recovery and in-situ disaster gas reduction: Insights from a micro perspective
detail.abstract: Driven by the dual factors of the continuous global surge in demand for unconventional natural gas and the escalating risks associated with coal mine gas, gas management has become increasingly crucial. Nevertheless, the low-permeability nature of coal seams severely constrains gas extraction efficiency. Based on Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), X-ray diffraction (XRD), microscopic observation, and low-temperature gas adsorption methods, this study investigates the influence of environmentally friendly modifiers on the microstructures of coal (including functional groups, crystallite parameters, 2D/3D surface morphologies, and pore-fracture information) and reveals the underlying mechanisms by which these microstructural evolutions regulate gas adsorption and migration behaviors in coal. The results shown that modification helps to reshape the microstructure of coal, reducing the hydroxyl group content in coal, breaking aliphatic side chains, and decreasing branching parameters. Concurrently, it is accompanied by an increase in methyl/ether bond content and a decrease in methylene content, and dissolution promotes the transformation of micropores to mesopores-macropores. In terms of morphology, modification alleviates mineral particle blockage, promotes surface leveling and crack opening of coal, and newly generated microcracks and dissolution pores enhance pore-crack connectivity, reducing fluid flow resistance. Gas adsorption testing confirmed that the number of super micropores in the range of 0.43-0.63 nm decreased after modification, weakening the gas adsorption capacity. Mesopores evolved to larger pores and reduced heterogeneity, thereby enhancing gas transport capacity. Further proposing the integrated strategy of ground and underground collaborative modification and pore pressure reduction can actively regulate the evolution of coal microstructure, promote gas migration, and achieve passive reduction of pore pressure, providing a new approach for efficient recovery of coalbed methane and gas hazard mitigation.

title: Impairments of Investment Securities by Nonfinancial Firms
affiliations: University of Connecticut - Department of Accounting, City University of New York (CUNY) - Stan Ross Department of Accountancy and University of Connecticut - Department of Accounting

detail.title: Impairments of Investment Securities by Nonfinancial Firms
detail.abstract: We study other-than-temporary impairments (OTTI) of investment securities in nonfinancial firms. Although these firms hold debt and equity securities, accounting rules and related academic research focus predominantly on financial institutions. We document the frequency and nature of OTTI among S&P 1,500 nonfinancial firms during 2000-2013. Exploring the recognition drivers in the relevant rules, we find that, consistent with the objective of regulation in effect during the period, the propensity to report OTTI is associated with variables capturing the likelihood of having impaired investments and the intent and ability to hold these investments to recovery. We find no evidence of opportunistic reporting. We also document an association between OTTI and earnings announcement returns, suggesting investors found the recognition of OTTI informative. Finally, we provide preliminary evidence that nonfinancial firms may have restructured their investment holdings in response to the promulgation of ASU 2016-01 and ASU 2016-13, which modified the accounting for investment securities for all public US firms. Our findings contribute to the cost-benefit discussion of industry-agnostic versus sector-specific standards.

title: The Role of Institutions in Shaping Fiscal Decentralization

detail.title: The Role of Institutions in Shaping Fiscal Decentralization
detail.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between institutional quality and fiscal decentralization, focusing on factors such as electoral processes, political pluralism, rule of law, corruption, and regulatory quality. Using a mixed-method approach, it combines panel data regressions with case studies from multiple countries. Results show that strong institutional frameworks significantly enhance fiscal decentralization, with improvements in governance, political stability, and accountability playing key roles. Lower corruption levels further reinforce these effects. The study concludes that strengthening democratic institutions and governance mechanisms is crucial for achieving effective and sustainable local fiscal autonomy, offering practical insights for policymakers aiming to implement institutional reforms.

title: Tourism in the Himalayan Kingdoms: Comparative Perspectives from Nepal and Bhutan
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Tourism in the Himalayan Kingdoms: Comparative Perspectives from Nepal and Bhutan
detail.abstract: This study examines tourism development in the Himalayan kingdoms of Nepal and Bhutan through a comparative perspective. Although geographically proximate and culturally linked by Buddhist traditions, the two countries have pursued markedly different approaches to tourism policy. Nepal has adopted an open-access, market-driven model that emphasizes maximizing arrivals, making it a global hub for trekking and mountaineering. Bhutan, by contrast, follows a "high value, low volume" strategy rooted in the philosophy of Gross National Happiness, prioritizing cultural preservation and environmental sustainability over mass participation. Using a qualitative case study design, the research draws on secondary sources including government policy documents, academic literature, international reports, and tourism statistics. The analysis explores three key dimensions: policy orientation, sustainability outcomes, and external influences such as geopolitics and climate change. Findings indicate that Nepal's model provides broad economic opportunities but suffers from environmental degradation, cultural commodification, and vulnerability to external shocks. Bhutan's restrictive framework has preserved cultural identity and ecosystems but faces limitations in inclusivity, diversification, and long-term resilience. The comparison highlights the trade-offs between accessibility and sustainability, underscoring that there is no universal model for tourism development. Instead, both cases demonstrate the importance of context-specific strategies that align tourism with broader societal values.

title: Behavioral Prompting: A Mechanism for Injecting Cognitive Style and Affective Patterns into Large Language Models

detail.title: Behavioral Prompting: A Mechanism for Injecting Cognitive Style and Affective Patterns into Large Language Models

detail.abstract: While modern prompt engineering offers significant control over the topic and format of Large Language Model (LLM) outputs, achieving deep and consistent control over nuanced persona traits such as cognitive style and affective patterns remains a significant challenge. Current methods are often brittle and fail to maintain a stable persona throughout an interaction. This paper introduces Behavioral Prompting, a novel framework for injecting a deep, predictable, and persistent persona into the generative process of any LLM. Our core contribution is a mechanism that architecturally decouples the task (the "what") from the persona (the "how"). This is achieved by systematically constructing a "meta-prompt" that combines the user's query with a structured "Personality Directive." This directive is a set of explicit, machine-readable instructions dynamically generated from a compact, pre-trained Behavioral Preference Model (B.P.M.), such as a LoRA adapter. We formalize the entire framework, from the definition of the B.P.M. to the final metaprompt construction. We argue that Behavioral Prompting is not a domain-specific solution, but a general-purpose mechanism for controllable text generation with broad applications in maintaining consistent brand voice, creating dynamic video game NPCs, and deploying personalized educational agents. This work represents a significant step towards a more robust and modular approach to persona management in generative AI.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces the Rural Innovation Equilibrium (RIE), a new economic theory proposing that sustainable and decentralized growth in rural economies can be achieved through innovation ecosystems rooted in local human capital, cooperative enterprise, and behavioral motivation. It challenges the dominance of centralized industrial models that treat rural regions as passive recipients of development, arguing instead for the recognition of innovation as a renewable factor of production. The theory defines equilibrium as the state where innovation output and capital retention within rural communities equal or exceed the inflow of external subsidies or urban dependency. The model integrates behavioral economics, Schumpeterian innovation theory, and institutional economics to form a mathematical and social framework for balancing productivity, autonomy, and equity. A practical model—the Rural Innovation Ecosystem (RIEc)—illustrates how workforce segmentation into Makers, Enablers, and Connectors creates a circular economy through localized production, distributed technology, and reinvestment. This structure transforms rural regions from consumption-based entities into innovation-generating systems capable of sustaining growth independently. Through its application to developing economies, particularly India, RIE offers a unifying perspective for economic revival that fuses technology, cooperative ownership, and intrinsic motivation. The model’s policy implications align with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) emphasizing education, employment, equity, and sustainability.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes an anchored, piecewise allocation rule to share the annual Blue Nile flow observed at the Ethiopia-Sudan border in the El Diem and GERD reach. The AB ESTUR rule sets an Ethiopian development anchor A equal to 28.8 BCM per year and uses a pivot M equal to 49 BCM per year, the long-term mean border flow. The rule maps the observed annual border flow F to three entitlements. If F is less than A, Ethiopia receives F while Sudan and Egypt receive zero. If F is at least A but less than M, Ethiopia receives A and the remainder is shared 60 percent to Sudan and 40 percent to Egypt. If F is at least M, each state receives its allocation at F equal to M, namely 28.8, 12.12, and 8.08 BCM for Ethiopia, Sudan, and Egypt, plus an equal share of the surplus, F minus M, divided by 3. The design conserves mass, is continuous at F equal to A and F equal to M, and yields monotonic allocations for each state. AB ESTUR is presented as a Blue Nile specific border gauge framework that moves beyond Aswan-centred quota narratives. White Nile and Atbara flows are treated as contextual information and are not used in the algebra. Worked examples across 25 to 80 BCM, together with simple climate scaling tests, illustrate the drought protection, recovery, and surplus sharing regimes of the rule. The paper concludes that AB ESTUR can serve as a transparent and auditable baseline for post-filling cooperation on the Eastern Nile.

detail.abstract: The objective of this study was to investigate the impacts of climate change on the agricultural and economic activity of the state of Goiás. Climate change can affect society through two mechanisms: (1) changes in temperature and precipitation regimes; and (2) an increase in the incidence of extreme events (natural disasters, such as wildfires). Accordingly, two types of analyses were conducted. First, we investigated how the three main permanent and temporary crops produced in the state were affected by precipitation and temperature anomalies. Next, we analyzed the impacts of wildfires on productive and economic variables in Goiás. Overall, the results suggest that climate change has been affecting the state's economy. The evidence indicates that changes in temperature and precipitation regimes affect agricultural production, especially temporary crops. Moreover, the results show that the degree of agricultural technological development in municipalities may act as a mitigating factor for these effects. In the case of wildfires, the estimates indicate negative effects in affected municipalities on several productive variables, such as: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and sectoral Gross Value Added (GVA); yields of permanent and temporary crops; the size of equine and cattle herds; milk production; and the number of firms and total employment links, including those in the Agricultural Sector.

detail.abstract: Contemporary science, armed with big data and artificial intelligence, has achieved unprecedented success in describing what a person does, yet the fundamental question of who a person is remains outside existing paradigms. We argue that the dominant approach of "Dataism," which reduces personality to its digital traces, is a form of reductionism incapable of modeling the generative core of the human self. This methodological gap requires the establishment of a new scientific discipline. In this manifesto, we formally declare the founding of Computational Personality Science, a new interdisciplinary field dedicated to the systematic observation, modeling, evaluation, and governance of a simulated human personality. We present a coherent methodological framework for this science, comprised of five foundational pillars: A. Observation: Ethical, "in-the-wild" data collection via Federated Longitudinal Studies (FLS). B. Modeling: Representing the self through a hybrid AI architecture (the "Mind-Soul" model). C. Interaction: Bringing models to life via Behavioral Prompting. D. Evaluation: Measuring authenticity via the "Personality Test." E. Governance: Ensuring sovereignty via the "Digital Will." Collectively, these pillars represent the first comprehensive methodology for moving from the analysis of behavioral data to the direct modeling of personality. We present a research agenda for this new science and call for broad interdisciplinary collaboration. Computational Personality Science opens the next chapter in humanity's long journey toward scientific selfknowledge.

detail.abstract: Rising political polarization generates significant negative externalities for democratic institutions and economic stability, yet scalable interventions to reduce polarization remain scarce. In this paper, I study whether AI chatbots can reduce political polarization. In two preregistered online RCTs with representative U.S. samples, I find that AI significantly reduces polarization on the Ukraine war and immigration policy. In Experiment 1, AI reduced polarization by 20 percentage points, with effects persisting for one month. Experiment 2 pits AI against incentivized human persuaders and Static Text. I find no significant difference in effectiveness: all three reduced polarization by roughly 10 percentage points. While AI conversations were rated as more enjoyable, mechanism analysis reveals that persuasion is driven by learning and trust, not enjoyment. These results demonstrate AI's scalable persuasive power, highlighting its dual-use potential: it can be deployed to effectively reduce polarization, but also poses risks of misuse.

detail.abstract: We study a 2018 reform in South Korea that reduced tax credits for automation investments. This reform increased the tax cost of investing in robots and thus resembles a robot tax. Exploiting this natural experiment with industry-level data on robot installations and firm-level data from Orbis, we document a sharp decline in automation investments after the reform in industries with a large share of affected firms. At the firm level, we find that affected firms increased employment, consistent with the notion that robots replaced workers. The effects are heterogeneous: financially constrained firms cut investment overall, while unconstrained firms substituted away from robots, hired more workers, and reallocated resources toward more productive uses. For the latter group, we find improvements in various measures of investment quality, suggesting that the tax credit induced inefficient overinvestment in automation. Our evidence informs ongoing debates on robot taxation and the efficiency of tax incentives.

detail.abstract: As companies reach maturity, typically beyond 20-30 years of operation, they often face stagnation in innovation, adaptability, and competitiveness. To sustain long-term economic dynamism, such corporations could be transitioned into non-profit organization (NPOs) and venture capital (VCs) entities. This conversion would enable them to redirect accumulated resources, expertise, and networks into supporting emerging start-ups, thereby fostering innovation and market competition.As corporations reach maturity, they frequently encounter systemic stagnation characterized by diminished innovation, bureaucratic inertia, and a focus on sustaining existing products over pioneering breakthroughs. This paper proposes a transformative pathway to repurpose these "corporate giants" into catalysts for future economic dynamism: their conversion into hybrid entities combining a Non-Profit Organization (NPO) and a Venture Capital (VC) arm. This structural shift enables mature firms to redirect their accumulated capital, extensive expertise, and vast networks toward funding and nurturing emerging start-ups, thereby reinvigorating market competition and innovation ecosystems.The successful execution of this transformation requires a robust framework built on core principles of trust and transparency in capital allocation, anti-discrimination to ensure equitable access for diverse entrepreneurs, and accountability to safeguard broader societal interests. We delineate a comprehensive roadmap for this conversion, addressing critical dimensions including the legal and regulatory mechanics of restructuring, the financial engineering of hybrid capital structures, and the design of governance models that balance fiduciary duties with social responsibility. The paper further explores operational redesign, cultural change leadership, and the development of an investment thesis that balances financial returns with measurable social impact.By embedding these values and mechanisms, the conversion of aging corporations into NPO-VC hybrids offers a systemic solution to corporate senescence. It transforms entities from defenders of legacy markets into guardians of the entrepreneurial ecosystem, ensuring that accumulated corporate wealth serves as a perpetual engine for sustainable, inclusive, and ethical growth in the global economy.

detail.abstract: The conventional view is that information leakage puts a firm at a disadvantage by limiting its ability to manage its information environment. In contrast, this study demonstrates that the possibility of leakage can sometimes enhance firm value. When an informed firm has the option to disclose, other supply chain participants fear adverse selection, attributing silence by the firm as indicative of the firm concealing news advantageous to them. This distrust can lead participants to take actions that are detrimental to the firm. The possibility of information leakage, then, benefits the firm by allaying these adverse selection concerns and fostering decisions among supply chain participants that are more favorable for the firm. Specifically, this study examines how voluntary disclosures and unintentional leakage combine to create an information environment that enables a firm to optimally curtail a potential rival's entry and manage a supplier's pricing terms.

title: Sectoral Divergence after a Shock: Wage Inequality and the Real Effects of Uzbekistan's 2017 Currency Liberalization

detail.title: Sectoral Divergence after a Shock: Wage Inequality and the Real Effects of Uzbekistan's 2017 Currency Liberalization
detail.abstract: This paper provides a causal estimate of the economic effects of Uzbekistan's September 2017 currency liberalization, a landmark reform that devalued the official exchange rate by nearly 50% and ended a long-standing dual-rate regime. Using an industrylevel panel dataset from 2010 to 2024, we employ a Difference-inDifferences (DiD) and event study methodology to analyze the reform's impact on real wages. We define "treated" industries as those with high exposure to international trade and capital mobility (Information & Communication, Finance, Industry) and "control" industries as those primarily oriented toward the domestic, non-tradable sector (Education, Health, Accommodation). Our results reveal a substantial and statistically significant divergence: real wages in the treated group grew approximately 30.8% faster relative to the control group. Crucially, we find no corresponding divergence in employment levels, suggesting the adjustment occurred primarily through prices rather than quantities. Our findings are robust to a series of specification checks and are validated by a placebo test. This study highlights the powerful, heterogeneous consequences of macroeconomic stabilization policies and underscores the critical role of sectoral characteristics in mediating the real effects of exchange rate shocks. These findings suggest that policymakers should consider sectoral disparities when implementing currency reforms.

detail.abstract: Concerned about the power that social media now wield, a chorus of tech-minded reformers have called for a return to the internet’s foundational design principles of interoperability and end-user control. This group argues for “middleware”—online tools like browser extensions and consumer-facing protocols that would enable people to take control of their online experiences across the web. This article argues that the campaign for middleware is laudable but mostly speculative and inapposite. It proceeds on the disproven theory that consumers can control their online experiences in today’s networked information economy. As such, it distracts reformers from solutions that would redress the structural asymmetries that define today’s market for consumer-facing services, including social media. This article argues that it is time to give up the illusory promise of user control and attend above all to enacting enforceable restrictions on service designs and commercial surveillance practices.

detail.abstract: Predictive technologies increasingly generate experiences that feel like meaningful coincidences: a recommendation that appears at precisely the right moment, an advertisement that echoes an unspoken thought, or a dream cue that feels uncannily relevant. This Article terms these engineered experiences algorithmic synchronicities—moments in which computational systems create the illusion of significance by anticipating users’ thoughts, emotions, or imagery with sufficient precision and timing to appear meaningful. Using synchronicity in its descriptive sense as a meaningful coincidence, rather than as a metaphysical claim, the Article argues that law lacks a vocabulary for recognizing these experiences as a form of manipulation rather than mere personalization. It proposes algorithmic synchronicity as a doctrinal and evidentiary tool for identifying meaning-based privacy and consumer harms that evade notice-and-choice frameworks.

title: Pressing Terrestrial Issues Versus Space Exploration: An Economic Lens

detail.title: Pressing Terrestrial Issues Versus Space Exploration: An Economic Lens
detail.abstract: How can large corporations and governments balance space exploration with pressing issues on Earth within an economic lens? This debate arises because opinions differ on whether funds should prioritize terrestrial issues like poverty and climate change or the exploration of space. Governments and corporations face challenges in decision making, as not all stakeholders,which for this issue include governments, private space companies such as SpaceX, taxpayers, economists, policymakers, and environmental advocates, agree on funding allocation. From an economic perspective, space exploration offers potential through resource collection and colonization on an alternate planet. However, the cost as well as the consumption of resources becomes a challenge. Conversely, investing in Earth’s preservation presents a compelling argument due to its widespread impact. Comparing the economic benefits of space exploration to the investment of funds to issues on Earth poses a challenge because of how many different perspectives there are, although there is a possibility of a viable solution.

title: Deciphering Football Spectator No-Show Behavior: Insights from Bundesliga and Bundesliga 2 Matches in Germany

detail.title: Deciphering Football Spectator No-Show Behavior: Insights from Bundesliga and Bundesliga 2 Matches in Germany
detail.abstract: This essay analyzes football spectator no-show behavior in Germany’s Bundesliga and 2. Bundesliga, focusing on how reported attendance can diverge from actual turnstile counts and why that gap matters for club revenue, stadium atmosphere, and demand estimation. Building on recent empirical work, I synthesize evidence that no-shows are systematically related to match characteristics (kick-off time, opponent quality, expected competitiveness), fan costs (travel distance, weather), and institutional features (season-ticket prevalence, resale frictions, and capacity constraints). I discuss how these factors bias standard demand models and can mislead pricing and operations decisions when clubs rely on tickets distributed rather than spectators present. I also assess policy responses—dynamic pricing tied to realized demand, easier verified resale, targeted nudges to season-ticket holders, and improved reporting standards—and outline implications for competitive balance and broadcast value. Overall, accounting for no-show behavior refines our understanding of football demand and yields more accurate guidance for clubs and leagues.

title: Four Questions about the Distributional Effects of Climate Policy
affiliations: Leipzig University and Uppsala University, Dept. of Economics

detail.title: Four Questions about the Distributional Effects of Climate Policy
detail.abstract:
Addressing the distributional effects of climate policy is one of the key challenges for securing a just and successful transition to carbon neutrality. Leaning on a large body of research, this paper answers four questions pertinent to understanding and counteracting the distributional effects of climate policy: 1) Why are the distributional effects of climate policy important? 2) Why do they arise? 3) What compensatory mechanisms and tools exist? 4) Which compensatory tools should be used? Our focus is on national, intragenerational distributional effects and policy.

We demonstrate that, while previous research has primarily examined the distributional effects of carbon pricing, the transition to carbon neutrality, which we refer to as the “climate transition,” generates numerous other distributional effects that are largely understudied. We further highlight that what makes the climate transition different from other technological transitions is that it affects households’ costs, e.g., via carbon pricing, rather than households’ income through, e.g., job loss. This implies that welfare systems in most countries, which are geared towards handling income shocks, are not well-equipped to handle the distributional effects of climate policy. Our mapping reveals, at least tentatively, that those households and individuals who bear the highest relative costs of climate policy (rural, low-income households) are also those who reap less of its material and health benefits and care the least about mitigating global climate damage for intergenerational sustainability. This observation, along with welfare systems that fail to adjust to cost shocks, may rationalize the political backlash.

We conceptually posit three desirable characteristics for compensatory measures: they should be efficient, precisely targeted, and visible. We evaluate the policy toolkit based on these characteristics and illustrate how achieving them may be mutually exclusive. While there exist potent and common tools to compensate low-income households, e.g., progressive income taxes, the tools for compensating for the geographical distributional effects are scarce and may imply inefficiencies. In summary, our review identifies several gaps in the current scientific literature and provides a mapping of available policies to help policymakers decide on when and why to use different measures.

title: Release Behavior and Risk Assessment of Heavy Metals from Nitric Acid Leach Residue of Phosphate Ore

detail.title: Release Behavior and Risk Assessment of Heavy Metals from Nitric Acid Leach Residue of Phosphate Ore
detail.abstract: Nitric acid-based wet-process phosphoric acid production has emerged as an industry priority for resource efficiency and environmental sustainability, yet heavy metal control in its byproduct-acid leaching residue-remains a critical bottleneck for safe disposal and valorization. This study systematically elucidated environmental behavior and health risks of heavy metals through mineralogical characterization, dynamic leaching experiments, and multi-dimensional risk assessment. Results revealed quartz, fluorite, and magnesium phosphate as dominant crystalline phases coexisting with amorphous silicates. Among hazardous elements (As, Cr, Pb, Hg, Cd), arsenic leachate exceeded GB 18599-2020 limits; cadmium and arsenic exhibited elevated labile fractions with pronounced short-term mobility risk, whereas lead, mercury, and chromium were predominantly residual, implying attenuated immediate risk. Leaching experiments unveiled a 'rapid dissolution-diffusion controlled' release pattern reaching dynamic equilibrium within 7 days under deionized water; acid conditions triggered a 'delayed surge' in As, Cr, and Pb. Ecological risk ranking was Hg > Cd > As > Cr > Pb, with mercury posing maximal threat. Health risk assessment confirmed carcinogenic risks from Cr, Pb, Cd, and As to both children and adults, with As as the principal contributor. Collectively, despite classification as non-hazardous waste, acid leaching residue poses substantial heavy metal-associated hazards, necessitating risk mitigation via solidification or extraction prior to realizing its P, K, and N-rich valorization potential. This study furnishes a robust theoretical foundation for safe disposal and resource utilization.

detail.abstract: There is a large academic literature that addresses whether patents are good measures of the innovations they cover. A related question that the literature has not addressed is whether existing patents are reliable predictors of future innovation in technological areas covered by the patents. The answer to this question is relevant to studies that might attempt to predict firm performance or the consequences of mergers or other conduct on innovation. detail.abstract: We document home-market advantage in European automobile markets and its interaction with the EV transition. Using brand-by-country monthly registrations for the EU27, 2014–2022, matched to statute-dated EV policy episodes (subsidies, bonus–malus, scrappage), we estimate PPML and market-share models with saturated fixed effects, Sun– Abraham event-time designs—including a triple difference (DDD)—and border-pair fixed effects. Three findings emerge. First, baseline home-market advantages are considerable across fuels. Second, around national EV policy onsets, extensive and intensive margins diverge: overall EV sales surge, but domestic brands’ within-brand EV shares fall by roughly 6–13 percentage points, and the Domestic × EV effect turns negative, reaching about −17 pp by year three under clean pre-trends. Third, heterogeneity is pronounced — effects are more potent in producer, richer, and infrastructure-dense markets. We interpret this as an incumbency disadvantage during technological transition: policies expand EV demand, yet foreign EV specialists capture a disproportionate share.

detail.abstract: The world faces a pressing challenge to meet key development objectives amid slowing growth and rising macroeconomic and geopolitical risks. With the number of job seekers rising rapidly, infrastructure shortfalls continuing to be large, and climate costs mounting, the case for a significant investment push has never been stronger. Yet the capacity to respond in many emerging market and developing economies (EMDEs) has eroded. Since the global financial crisis, investment growth has slowed to about half its pace in the 2000s, with both public and private investment weakening. Foreign direct investment inflows—a critical source of capital, technology, and managerial know-how—have also fallen sharply and become increasingly concentrated, leaving low-income countries (LICs) with only a marginal share. The risks of further retrenchment are significant, as trade tensions, policy uncertainty, and elevated debt levels continue to weigh on investment. Reigniting momentum will require ambitious domestic reforms to strengthen institutions, rebuild macro-fiscal stability, and deepen trade and investment integration—the foundations of a supportive business climate. At the same time, international cooperation is indispensable. A renewed commitment to a predictable system of cross-border trade and investment flows, combined with scaled-up financial support and sustained technical assistance, is essential to help EMDEs—especially LICs and economies in fragile and conflict situations—bridge financing gaps and implement the domestic reforms needed to restore investment as an engine of growth, jobs, and development.

detail.title: Winners and Losers: Competition, Creative Destruction, and Labor Income Risk
detail.abstract: Using U.S. administrative data, we find that technology-driven creative destruction in the product market passes through to worker earnings. The passthrough to incumbent worker earnings is both asymmetric and concentrated: profit drops from rival innovations lead to proportionally greater earning declines and changes in the likelihood of job destruction than profit gains from their own firm's innovations, while top workers are significantly more exposed than the average worker. We develop an endogenous-growth model with monopsonistic labor markets and worker heterogeneity that replicates this asymmetry and the distribution of earnings risk. Creative destruction exposes high-income workers to concentrated downside risk while offering lower-income workers upward mobility, shaping the welfare consequences of innovation policy.

title: The Name Game: How Contractual Form, Not Reserve Ratios, Defines Money

detail.title: The Name Game: How Contractual Form, Not Reserve Ratios, Defines Money
detail.abstract: For nearly a century, the Austrian School has been fractured by the seemingly intractable debate over fractional-reserve banking (FRB), pitting proponents of a 100% reserve requirement, who view FRB as institutionalized fraud, against free-banking advocates, who see it as a legitimate market innovation. This paper argues that this entire debate is rooted in a fundamental category mistake: it has treated a problem of jurisprudence and contract law as if it were a matter of economic theory. We demonstrate through a thought experiment—termed "the name game"—that any legal prohibition against fractional-reserve banking is practically futile. The market, driven by the persistent demand for interest-bearing liquid assets, will inevitably circumvent such a restriction by re-creating the same economic function under a new institutional form (e.g., a "loan fund" instead of a "bank"). This phenomenon is not merely theoretical, as evidenced by the historical emergence of money market funds and the shadow banking system to bypass financial regulations. The conclusion is stark: the war against FRB was a semantic one, and the market has already won. The true locus of analysis, therefore, must shift from the institution to the instrument—from the "bank" to the "contract." This paper contends that the valid concerns of both the Rothbardian and free-banking camps can be reconciled under a new, unified framework centered on contractual clarity and honest labeling. The real issue is not the reserve ratio, but whether a financial instrument is honestly represented as a secure bailment or an at-risk investment. By re-founding the debate on this contractual-legal basis, we can transcend the historical deadlock and unite the Austrian School against its true enemy: the systemic contractual opacity fostered by the modern, state-backed financial system.

detail.abstract:
Banks must extract useful signals of a potential borrower’s quality from a large set of possibly informative characteristics when making lending decisions. A model that speaks to how banks specialize in lending to an industry in order to better extract signals from data, can potentially be applied to a number of real-world scenarios. In this post, we apply lessons from such a model to a topic of timely relevance in economics: job market recommendation letters. Institutions looking to hire new economists must evaluate PhD applicants based on limited and often noisy signals of future performance, including letters of recommendation from these applicants’ advisors or co-authors. Using insights from our model, we argue that the value of these letters depends on who reads them.

detail.title: Collaboration between Village-Owned Enterprises and the Private Sector in Sustainable Village Tourism Development through the PPP-DBFOM Scheme: A Case Study of Kutuh Village, Badung Regency
detail.abstract: This study analyzes the collaboration between Village-Owned Enterprises (BUMDes) and the private sector in the development of sustainable village tourism through the application of a Public-Private Partnership (PPP) scheme with a Design-Build-Finance-Operate-Maintain (DBFOM) model. The approach used is a conceptual literature review by reviewing more than 15 relevant national and international journals, as well as secondary sources from institutions such as the OECD, World Bank, and UNWTO. The analysis focuses on the integration of collaborative governance, new public governance, public accountability, and creating shared value (CSV) theories to formulate a conceptual framework for collaboration at the village level. The results of the study show that the success of BUMDes-Private collaboration is determined by four main factors: (1) transparent and participatory collaborative governance, (2) trust and communication between actors, (3) fair distribution of risks and benefits, and (4) institutional capacity and managerial innovation of BUMDes. The case study of Kutuh Village, Badung Regency, Bali, serves as an empirical illustration that confirms the effectiveness of the PPP-DBFOM model on a micro scale. Collaboration in this village has succeeded in increasing economic efficiency, strengthening local institutions, and promoting socio-environmental sustainability through the application of benefit-sharing principles and community participation. Conceptually, the results of this study expand the application of PPP in the context of the village economy by emphasizing the importance of collaborative governance based on shared values. These findings also provide policy implications for strengthening the capacity of BUMDes, adaptive contract design, and the formulation of public policies that support cross-sector collaboration towards inclusive and sustainable village tourism development.

I triangulate my estimates with national accounts aggregates and previous work on Belgian wealth inequality. The evolution of Belgian wealth inequality is in line with other European countries for which long-run estimates are available.

detail.abstract: This study highlights the multifaceted nature of household payment task division, revealing that a broad spectrum of factors contributes to who takes the lead in executing household payments. The allocation of specific payment tasks is related to partners’ differences in personality traits, enjoyment of payment tasks and available time. Disparities in income and assets also play a significant role, alongside differences in payment knowledge, digital payment experience, and money management skills. Furthermore, individuals tend to replicate the division of payment tasks observed in others. Traditional patterns whereby men manage housing-related payments and women handle grocery expenses, appear across all generations but are most prevalent among the oldest. Greater involvement in household payment tasks is associated with increased financial influence within the household. It also facilitates the ability to take over a partner’s payment responsibilities when needed and enhances early awareness of potential financial issues. In a substantial number of households, one partner is solely responsible for managing specific payments. Strong payment knowledge, digital payment experience, and staying informed about the partner’s payment activities support a smooth transition of responsibilities when necessary.

detail.abstract: The advantages of adaptive experiments have led to their rapid adoption in economics, other fields, as well as among practitioners. However, adaptive experiments pose challenges for causal inference. This note suggests a BOLS (batched ordinary least squares) test statistic for inference of treatment effects in adaptive experiments. The statistic provides a precisionequalizing aggregation of per-period treatment-control differences under heteroskedasticity. The combined test statistic is a normalized average of heteroskedastic per-period z-statistics and can be used to construct asymptotically valid confidence intervals. We provide simulation results comparing rejection rates in the typical case with few treatment periods and few (or many) observations per batch.

detail.title: Tourism as a Driver of Economic Transformation: Pathways Toward Sustainable and Inclusive Growth in the Maldives
detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of tourism as a catalyst for economic transformation in the Maldives, a small island developing state where tourism constitutes the backbone of national income, employment, and foreign exchange. Over the past four decades, the sector has evolved from a luxury niche market into a diversified and resilient component of the Maldivian economy. Drawing on policy analysis, institutional reports, and comparative evidence, the study explores how tourism has driven infrastructure expansion, human capital development, and regional integration. It also highlights the growing emphasis on sustainability and inclusiveness as core pillars of national development strategies. The findings suggest that while tourism has successfully propelled economic growth, it also poses environmental and social challenges-ranging from ecosystem degradation to spatial inequality. The paper argues that achieving long-term resilience requires embedding green innovation, local empowerment, and climate adaptation into the tourism model. The Maldivian case provides valuable insights into how small economies can leverage tourism for sustainable and inclusive transformation in a globalized world.

detail.abstract: Italy's economy has been characterized by a long-standing malaise marked by low growth, stagnant productivity, and high public debt. In recent years, these weaknesses have been compounded by declining real wages, the underutilization and outward migration of skilled labor, widening territorial disparities, and a rise in income and wealth inequality. The country's productive structure remains concentrated in traditional sectors, dominated by small firms, and underrepresented in strategic industries with high potential for productivity gains. Drawing on macroeconomic and sectoral evidence, this policy brief assesses Italy's current position and outlines the measures needed to reverse these trends. It argues for an industrial strategy that combines state-market complementarities, long-term coordination, and polycentric governance, supported by policies to halt real wage decline and reduce inequality, with the aim of rebuilding productive capacity and ensuring broadly shared prosperity.

detail.title: Biodiversity preferences in urban environments: Full and partial choice experiment profiles with participatory GIS
detail.abstract: Biodiversity policies have emerged around the world to address the losses to nature from economic and urban development. In this paper, we aim to determine residents’ preferences for increased biodiversity as part of urban (re)developments, where they want to experience more biodiversity, and the extent in which their preferences differentiate by species. The empirical approach incorporates a comparison of full and partial attribute profiles in a split-sample discrete choice experiment (DCE) with Participatory Geographic Information Systems (PGIS) heat map debriefing questions. Our application is for Greater Manchester, United Kingdom against the background of the Biodiversity Net Gain policy (BNG) in England. We investigate attribute attendance, magnitude changes in mean estimates and follow up with covariate interaction effects on attributes using sociodemographic characteristics and PGIS derived distance variables. Our results indicate partial profiles enhance attribute attendance and the magnitudes of mean estimates vary between the full and partial profiles, but the order of preferences are relatively stable as the species with the highest and lowest mean estimates remain unchanged. In doing so we add to a strand of literature on people’s environmental preferences comparing full and partial profiles with the addition of practical and novel insights on self-reported location preferences. The mean estimates and location preferences are useful in the given BNG policy context to inform authorities and housing developers on residents’ preferences and locations for species enhancement. This in turn can help define priorities for urban green measure selection and land-use planning in the longer term.

detail.title: Electoral Influence of Newspapers in Switzerland (1896 -1917)
detail.abstract: This paper examines the influence of newspapers in federal elections in Switzerland between 1896 and 1917. Using a novel dataset covering 1,466 newspapers in this period, we analyze how newspaper entry and exit affected voter turnout and party vote shares across 49 constituencies. Our empirical strategy exploits discrete changes in the number of newspapers between election years within constituencies. We show that an increase in the number of political newspapers significantly induced a higher voter turnout. The political influence of German-language newspapers was statistically significant, whereas French-language newspapers played a limited role in shaping electoral outcomes. However, we find no robust evidence that partisan newspapers systematically benefited their affiliated parties' vote shares.

title: FREE IS NOT ENOUGH - THE LONG-RUN IMPACT OF FREE EDUCATION ON COGNITIVE FUNCTION IN OLDER AGE: EVIDENCE FROM IRELAND

detail.title: FREE IS NOT ENOUGH - THE LONG-RUN IMPACT OF FREE EDUCATION ON COGNITIVE FUNCTION IN OLDER AGE: EVIDENCE FROM IRELAND
detail.abstract: Dementia is a major and growing global health challenge, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where most of the worlds older population will reside in the coming decades. With no curative treatments available, prevention has come to the forefront, and education is repeatedly identified as one of the strongest protective correlates of late-life cognitive decline. Whether this relationship is causal, however, remains uncertain, as existing evidence has produced mixed findings.This paper investigates the long-term cognitive effects of expanded access to secondary education by exploiting the 1967 Irish Free Education reform. Using data from the Irish Longitudinal Study on Ageing (TILDA), we implement a regression discontinuity design based on quasi-random exposure to the reform by birth cohort.The reform substantially increased years of schooling, with the largest gainsnearly one additional yearamong individuals from low socioeconomic backgrounds. However, we find no evidence that these increases translated into improvements in global cognition, executive function, processing speed, or attention in older age, nor into better labour market or health behaviour outcomes that could serve as mediating pathways. Drawing on historical administrative records, we show that the reform triggered a rapid influx of students without commensurate investment in school infrastructure or teacher capacity, generating conditions consistent with declining educational quality. Our findings suggest that expanding access to education, while essential, may not be sufficient to produce long-term cognitive benefits unless accompanied by adequate investments in instructional quality, an insight highly relevant to countries currently expanding free secondary education.

detail.abstract: To support credit-constrained small businesses, governments use loan guarantee programs that insure lenders against default risk. However, these programs face challenges in allocating appropriate loan sizes due to limited information about small businesses. This paper explores the welfare implications of using a loan guarantee menu as a screening mechanism to address such challenges, in the context of the South Korean loan guarantee program. I investigate how offering a loan guarantee menu alongside soft information collection (e.g., interviews and site visits) encourages borrowers to reveal their private information, thereby enabling the government agency to make more informed loan size decisions. The study evaluates how these screening mechanisms impact both the economic output of small businesses and the financial losses incurred by the government, as captured by the agency’s objective function—a combination of these two outcomes. I find that a loan guarantee menu is effective on its own, increasing the value of the agency’s objective function by 3.9%. When combined with soft information collection, its impact is significantly enhanced, leading to an 8.7% increase. This complementarity arises because efforts to collect soft information encourage borrowers with varying risk profiles to self-select into appropriate contracts, thereby leading to more efficient loan allocations.

detail.abstract:
This article introduces the concept of economic bridges as dynamic, immigrant-led mechanisms that enhance the resilience of global value chains (GVCs) in niche markets amid geopolitical crises and supply disruptions. Drawing on an integrated theoretical framework combining GVC theory (Gereffi et al., 2005), the resource-based view (Barney, 1991), and social capital theory (Bourdieu, 1986), the study posits that these bridges structured through relational partnerships, logistical infrastructure, financial buffering, and innovation linkages facilitate bidirectional flows of resources, knowledge, and capital between host and origin economies. The primary problem addressed is the underexplored role of immigrant entrepreneurs in systemic GVC resilience, where literature has prioritized lead-firm governance over peripheral actor contributions, leaving gaps in cross-border impacts during uncertainty.

Employing a mixed-methods approach, including a qualitative case study with elements of quantitative analysis (e.g., financial audits, benchmarks from Omnisend and Klaviyo 2025 reports), the research examines an immigrant founded e-commerce venture in a U.S. niche market. Key findings reveal 20–30% enhancements in chain efficiency, as evidenced by 277% year-over-year growth, 38.8% customer retention (exceeding 25–30% industry averages), and annual economic returns surpassing 1.5 million USD to the origin economy through multiplicative effects (1:3 investment ratios in jobs, taxes, and development). These outcomes validate four hypotheses, demonstrating how bridges mitigate disruptions like those reducing global GDP by 1.5% in conflict scenarios, while fostering social sustainability through job preservation and inclusive growth.

The theoretical contribution lies in extending GVC models to incorporate migrant agency, filling gaps in resilience literature for niche contexts. Practically, the framework provides a step-by-step roadmap for immigrant SMBs to build bridges, emphasizing agility in crises. Policy implications include recommendations for governments to scale these into overseas export hubs, potentially generating billions in value for developing states by leveraging diaspora networks. Limitations, such as the single-case focus, suggest avenues for future longitudinal and comparative research. Overall, this work advances a paradigm for equitable, resilient GVCs, urging scholars and policymakers to harness immigrant entrepreneurship as a strategic asset in an interconnected world.

title: Just and green? Workers’ perspectives on Slovakia’s automotive transition

detail.title: Just and green? Workers’ perspectives on Slovakia’s automotive transition
detail.abstract: As global industries undergo rapid decarbonisation, questions of work, justice, and sustainability have become central to the politics of economic transformation. This paper examines the perspectives of blue-collar workers in Slovakia’s automotive industry as they navigate the transition toward electromobility. Drawing on Q methodology, the study identifies three distinct discourses that express diverse orientations toward sustainability, technological change, and the political role of labour in industrial transformation. These discourses reveal how workers’ understandings of ecological modernisation, economic security, and social justice are shaped by both structural dependencies and lived experiences of industrial change. Although marked by ambivalence or misunderstandings of labour-nature relations, the findings highlight the importance of recognising workers not merely as recipients of industrial and environmental policy but as active interpreters and participants. The paper contributes to a growing body of research that foregrounds labour agency and subjective meaning in socio-ecological transformations, underscoring the centrality of work in shaping pathways toward a sustainable and socially just future.

detail.abstract: This diploma thesis investigates the international transmission of fiscal-policy shocks across advanced economies. Using quarterly data for the United States, the Euro Area, the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, Japan, and Norway over 1980-2005, the study estimates structural vector autoregressions (SVARs) to identify exogenous government-spending shocks and trace their effects on output, consumption, investment, interest rates, exchange rates, and public debt. The analysis finds that domestic fiscal expansions generate positive but heterogeneous spillovers, with stronger effects through investment and weaker responses in consumption. Spillovers are more persistent under coordinated monetary-fiscal regimes and when fiscal shocks are investment-driven rather than consumption-driven. The results highlight the role of institutional and exchangerate arrangements in shaping fiscal multipliers and cross-border propagation. The study concludes that international policy coordination can enhance stabilization efficiency and reduce asymmetries in open-economy responses to government-spending shocks. detail.title: Factor Pricing in the Frequency Domain: Evidence from China
detail.abstract: This paper employs the frequency-dependent principal component analysis (PCA) approach to examine the stochastic discount factor (SDF) in China's A-share market. We find that the SDF exhibits pronounced sparsity in the low-frequency principal component space: a small number of low-frequency factors are sufficient to explain test asset returns and deliver an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio close to one, whereas high-frequency factors fail to achieve such sparsity. The low-frequency PCA factors do not exhibit a distinct advantage in long-only portfolios, but their performance in short portfolios is comparable to that in long-short portfolios, suggesting that the identified low-frequency components capture persistent mispricing associated with short-sale constraints. Finally, decomposing the low-frequency mean-variance efficient portfolio into a high-frequency risk component and a slow-moving component reveals that the slow-moving component experiences minimal drawdowns during crisis periods such as COVID-19 and significantly predicts future GDP growth, while the highfrequency component is closely related to innovations in investor sentiment.
